content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of artemether-lumefantrine for the treatment of uncomplicated malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum. This review aimed to assess the efficacy of the six-dose regimen of artemether-lumefantrine compared to other standard treatment regimens, as well as its performance in real-world clinical settings. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to April 2005. Conference proceedings, reference lists of relevant articles, and input from malaria experts and the pharmaceutical manufacturer of artemether-lumefantrine were also included. The review focused on randomized controlled trials that compared the six-dose regimen of artemether-lumefantrine with other standard treatments, either as monotherapy or in combination, and under both supervised and unsupervised conditions. The primary outcome of interest was the total treatment failure rate by day 28, with extended follow-up periods for certain comparator drugs (day 42 for sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and day 63 for mefloquine). Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were performed independently by two authors. The analysis included nine trials with a total of 4,547 participants. The results showed that the six-dose regimen of artemether-lumefantrine had a lower treatment failure rate by day 28 compared to amodiaquine (based on one trial with 270 participants) and amodiaquine combined with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (one trial with 507 participants). However, it did not demonstrate superiority over the combination of chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (two trials with 201 participants). When compared to other artemisinin-based combination therapies, artemether-lumefantrine was more effective than the combination of amodiaquine and artesunate (two trials with 668 participants). However, it was less effective than the combination of mefloquine and artesunate (four trials with 270 participants). No significant difference in efficacy was observed when compared to dihydroartemisinin-naphthoquine-trimethoprim (one trial with 89 participants). In conclusion, the six-dose regimen of artemether-lumefantrine appears to be more effective than antimalarial regimens that do not include artemisinin derivatives. Its performance relative to other artemisinin-based combination therapies varies depending on the specific comparator regimen.
